{{legend0|#F48984|Republican hold}} }} '''United States gubernatorial elections''' were held on November 7, 2023, in the states of [[Kentucky]] and [[Mississippi]], with an election having occurred in [[Louisiana]] on October 14. These elections form part of the [[2023 United States elections]]. The last regular gubernatorial elections for all three states were in [[2019 United States gubernatorial elections|2019]]. In Louisiana, term-limited incumbent [[John Bel Edwards]] was succeeded by [[Jeff Landry]], flipping the seat from [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] to [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] control. In Kentucky, Democrat [[Andy Beshear]] won re-election to a second term. In Mississippi, Republican [[Tate Reeves]] won re-election to a second term. == Partisan composition == Going into the election, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors in the United States. This class of governors was made up of 1 Republican and 2 Democrats. Democrats were defending two governorships in states [[Donald Trump]] won in 2020 (Kentucky and Louisiana).{{Cite web |last=Vakil |first=Caroline |date=2023-01-02 |title=Here are the governors' races to watch in 2023 |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/3791114-here-are-the-governors-races-to-watch-in-2023/ |access-date=2024-01-05 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |last=Jacobson |first=Louis |date=June 8, 2023 |title=Democrats Face Uphill Challenge in Three Off-Year Races for Governor |url=https://www.usnews.com/news/elections/articles/2023-06-08/democrats-face-uphill-challenge-in-three-off-year-races-for-governor |access-date=January 5, 2023 |work=[[US News & World Report]]}} ==Election predictions== Several sites and individuals published predictions of competitive seats. These predictions looked at factors such as the strength of the [[incumbent]] (if the incumbent is running for re-election), the strength of the candidates, and the partisan leanings of the state (reflected in part by the state's [[Cook Partisan Voting Index]] rating). The predictions assigned ratings to each seat, with the rating indicating a party's predicted advantage in winning that seat. Most election predictors use: * "tossup": no advantage * "tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean" * "lean": slight advantage * "likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage * "safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory {|class="wikitable sortable" |- valign=bottom ! He was [[Term limits in the United States#Gubernatorial term limits|term-limited]] by the [[Constitution of Louisiana|Louisiana Constitution]] in 2023, and could not seek reelection for a third consecutive term. Louisiana utilizes a [[jungle primary]] system. Republican [[List of Attorneys General of Louisiana|Attorney General]] [[Jeff Landry]] was considered the frontrunner. Other candidates included [[Louisiana State Senate|state senator]] [[Sharon Hewitt]], and [[Louisiana State Treasurer|Treasurer]] [[John Schroder]]. Democratic Secretary of Transportation [[Shawn Wilson (politician)|Shawn Wilson]] also ran to succeed Edwards.{{cite web |last=Karlin|first=Sam|title=Billy Nungesser to announce he's not running for governor, will seek re-election |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/elections/billy-nungesser-to-announce-hes-not-running-for-governor-will-seek-re-election/article_5cd6018a-9053-11ed-9089-678da36fdfa2.html|website=The Advocate|date=9 January 2023|access-date=11 January 2023}}{{cite news |last1=Doyle |first1=Matt |title=2023 Governor's race could be packed with GOP heavy hitters |url=https://louisianaradionetwork.com/2019/11/19/2023-governors-race-could-be-packed-with-gop-heavy-hitters/ |access-date=November 29, 2020 |work=[[Louisiana Radio Network]] |publisher=[[Louisiana Farm Bureau Federation]] |date=November 19, 2019}} Landry won with over 51% of the vote in the primary, becoming the first person to win a Louisiana gubernatorial election without a runoff since [[Bobby Jindal]] in [[2011 Louisiana gubernatorial election|2011]]. Landry easily prevailed over several Republican opponents and the leading Democratic candidate.{{cite news |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=October 14, 2023 |date=October 14, 2023 |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/10/14/jeff-landry-wins-louisiana-governor-00121598 |last=Montellaro |first=Zach |title=Landry wins Louisiana governor's race, flipping state red}} All the Republican candidates collectively won 65.52% of the vote, including a candidate who got 0.34% of the vote as he dropped out of the race but remained on the ballot. All the Democrats collectively won 28.53% of the vote, and all the Independents collectively won 5.95% of the vote. This was the only governorship to flip parties in the 2023 elections. {{Election box begin no change| title=2023 Louisiana gubernatorial election{{cite '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#AE8BB1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Kentucky|Governor]] | before_election = [[Andy Beshear]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Andy Beshear]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | last_update = | time_zone = | reporting = }} {{ElectionsKY}} The '''2023 Kentucky gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2023, to elect the [[Governor of Kentucky|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky|lieutenant governor]] of [[Kentucky]]. Incumbent [[Kentucky Democratic Party|Democratic]] governor [[Andy Beshear]] won re-election to a second term, defeating [[Republican Party of Kentucky|Republican]] [[Attorney General of Kentucky|state Attorney General]] [[Daniel Cameron (American politician)|Daniel Cameron]]. This was the only statewide victory in 2023 for Democrats in Kentucky, and one of only two nationwide. This race was one of two Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2023 in a state [[Donald Trump]] won in [[2020 United States presidential election in Kentucky|2020]]. The other was held in [[2023 Louisiana gubernatorial election|Louisiana]], where the incumbent Democratic governor was ineligible to seek re-election, and which [[Jeff Landry]] flipped for the Republicans. This was the first gubernatorial election in the state's history in which both major party candidates had held the position of attorney general; Beshear held the position from 2016 to 2019, after which he was succeeded by Cameron. Beshear's victory has been attributed to his broad popularity among Democrats and independents, as well as approximately half of Republicans in the state.{{Cite web |title=U.S. Governor Rankings: Beshear Gets a Boost, Desantis' Approval Dips |url=https://pro.morningconsult.com/analysis/governor-approval-ratings-july-2023 |access-date=November 8, 2023 |website=Morning Consult Pro |language=en |archive-date=November 7, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231107220729/https://pro.morningconsult.com/analysis/governor-approval-ratings-july-2023 |url-status=live }} Compared to 2019, Beshear most improved his performance in suburban precincts; he increased his margins by nearly 6 percentage points in suburban areas, compared to 4.5 percentage points in urban and rural precincts.{{Cite news |date=November 7, 2023 |title=Election 2023: Democrats win control of Va. legislature; Ohio residents vote to protect abortion rights |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/11/07/election-2023-live-updates/ |access-date=November 8, 2023 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en |archive-date=November 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231108044814/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/11/07/election-2023-live-updates/ |url-status=live }} == Background == A [[Social conservatism in the United States|socially conservative]] southern state, Kentucky is considered [[Red states and blue states|safely Republican]] in federal elections, with Republicans holding both of its U.S. Senate seats and all but one of its U.S. House seats. In the [[2020 United States presidential election in Kentucky|2020 presidential election]], Republican [[Donald Trump]] carried Kentucky by 26 percentage points. However, the state was much more competitive as recently as the 1990s, when it voted for [[Bill Clinton]] twice, and Democrats remain competitive in many local and some state-level elections. Beshear was first elected in [[2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election|2019]], narrowly defeating incumbent Republican [[Matt Bevin]], who had become widely unpopular for signing a [[2018 Kentucky Senate Bill 151|pension reform bill]] for teachers and opposing a subsequent teachers' strike. In that same year, Cameron was elected attorney general, becoming the first African-American to be elected to that position. Cameron gained national recognition as attorney general, especially due to his involvement in the [[Killing of Breonna Taylor|Breonna Taylor case]] in 2020. He spoke at the [[2020 Republican National Convention]] on August 25, 2020.{{Cite news |title=Daniel Cameron, Kentucky A.G., Speaks at the R.N.C.: Full Transcript |work=The New York Times |date=August {{legend0|#808080|No votes}} |Precinct results |default=1}} | map_caption = | turnout = 36.3% {{decrease}} | title = [[Louisiana|Governor]] | before_election = [[John Bel Edwards]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Jeff Landry]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) | image3 = }} {{Elections in Louisiana sidebar}} The '''2023 Louisiana gubernatorial election''' was held on October 14, 2023, to elect the [[List of governors of Louisiana|governor of Louisiana]]. Incumbent Governor [[John Bel Edwards]] was term-limited and could not seek re-election to a third consecutive term in office.{{cite web|url=http://senate.legis.state.la.us/documents/constitution/constitution.pdf|title=Louisiana Constitution of 1974|publisher=Government of Louisiana|access-date=January 14, 2021|archive-date=October 15, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231015001406/https://senate.legis.state.la.us/documents/constitution/constitution.pdf|url-status=dead}} This race was one of two Democratic-held governorships up for election in 2023 in a state that voted for [[Donald Trump]] in [[2020 United States presidential election in Louisiana|2020]]. Under Louisiana's [[Louisiana primary|two-round]] system, all candidates appear on the same ballot, regardless of party, and voters may vote for any candidate regardless of that person's party affiliation. If no candidate had received an absolute majority of the vote during the primary election on October 14, 2023, a runoff election would have been held on November 18, 2023, between the top two candidates in the primary.{{cite news |last1=Wilson |first1=Sabrina |title=How crowded will field get for Louisiana governor's race? |url=https://www.fox8live.com/2023/03/14/how-crowded-will-field-get-louisiana-governors-race/ |access-date=May 16, 2023 |work=[[WVUE-DT|WVUE]] |date=March 13, 2023}} State Attorney General [[Jeff Landry]] won with over 51% of the vote in the primary. This was the first time a candidate won a Louisiana gubernatorial election without a runoff since fellow Republican [[Bobby Jindal]] was re-elected in [[2011 Louisiana gubernatorial election|2011]]. Landry easily prevailed over several Republican opponents, including former state chamber of commerce CEO Stephen Waguespack and State Treasurer [[John Schroder]]. Former state Transportation Secretary [[Shawn Wilson]] was the leading Democratic candidate.{{cite news |work=[[Politico]] |access-date=October 14, 2023 |date=October 14, 2023 |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2023/10/14/jeff-landry-wins-louisiana-governor-00121598 |last=Montellaro |first=Zach |title=Landry wins Louisiana governor's race, flipping state red}} All the Republican candidates collectively won 65.52% of the vote, including a candidate who got 0.34% of the vote as he dropped out of the race but remained on the ballot. All the Democrats collectively won 28.53% of the vote, and all the Independents collectively won 5.95% of the vote. This was the only governorship to flip parties in the 2023 elections. {{TOC limit|2}} == Background == [[Louisiana]], like much of the [[Deep South]], is a [[Social conservatism in the United States|socially conservative]] "[[Bible Belt]]" state. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] were the favored party at all levels of government as recently as the 1990s; however, the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] has since rapidly gained ground, first at the federal level and gradually at the state and local level as well. Today, the state is strongly Republican-leaning and, at the time of the election, Republicans held both of the state's [[United States Senate|U.S. Senate]] seats, all but [[Louisiana's 2nd congressional district|one]] of its [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] [[Louisiana's congressional districts|seats]], majorities in both of its [[Louisiana State Legislature|state legislative chambers]], and every statewide executive office except the governorship, which they would ultimately win. [[John Bel Edwards]], a populist conservative Democrat, was able to win two terms as governor and overcome the state's partisan lean by diverging from the national party on certain policy matters, such as abortion, while also appealing to Louisiana's contemporary Democratic voting base.{{Cite web |title=Democratic Gov. John Bel Edwards wins reelection in Louisiana |url=https://www.politico.com/news/2019/11/16/louisiana-governor-race-edwards-rispone-071288 |access-date=2023-02-08 |date=November 16, 2019 |website=POLITICO |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=2021-04-20 |title=Democrat Edwards wins reelection in conservative Louisiana |url=https://apnews.com/article/john-bel-edwards-donald-trump-us-news-ap-top-news-politics-b65e73cbb2304514997d073a36e5bcbd |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=AP NEWS |language=en}} However, as Edwards was term-limited going into the election, most analysts expected the governorship to flip back to the Republican Party in 2023, primarily due to the lack of Democratic candidates with Edwards' crossover appeal.{{Cite web |title=2023 Odd Year Governor Race Ratings |url=https://www.cookpolitical.com/analysis/governors/governors-overview/2023-odd-year-governor-race-ratings |access-date=2023-02-08 |website=Cook Political Report |language=en}} This proved to be true as Republican [[Jeff Landry]] won the election in a landslide, with over 51% of the vote. Republicans collectively secured about 66% of the vote while Democrats won only about 29%, an all time low, with about 26% going to their top vote getter and runner up [[Shawn Wilson]]. ==Democratic candidates== ===Declared=== *Danny Cole, [[Pentecostalism|Pentecostal]] pastor{{cite web |last=Noakes |first=Alena|url=https://www.kalb.com/2023/02/15/cenla-resident-running-louisiana-governor/ | title=Cenla resident running for Louisiana governor |date=February 15, 2023 |website=KALB}} *[[Shawn Wilson]], former secretary of the [[Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development]]{{cite web | title=Former Louisiana DOTD Secretary Shawn Wilson announces his bid for governor | website=Fox 8 Live | date=March 6, 2023 | url=https://www.fox8live.com/2023/03/06/former-louisiana-dotd-secretary-shawn-wilson-announces-his-bid-governor/ | access-date=March 6, 2023}} ===Declined=== *[[Katie Bernhardt]], chair of the [[Louisiana Democratic Party]]{{cite news |url=https://kpel965.com/louisiana-democratic-chair-not-running-governor/ |work=KPEL965 |access-date=June 7, 2023 |title=After Controversial Viral Ad, Louisiana Democratic Chair Says She Isn't Running for Governor |last=Cunningham |first=Joe |date=February 13, 2023}} ''(endorsed Wilson)''{{Cite web |last=Bridges |first=Tyler |date=2023-04-01 |title=Katie Bernhardt, no longer facing challenge to her job, says Democrats face brighter days |url=https://www.nola.com/news/politics/katie-bernhardt-now-secure-as-state-democratic-party-chair/article_5d283f1a-d0ca-11ed-80a8-933d33aaa7a1.html |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=NOLA.com |language=en}} *[[Sharon Weston Broome]], [[mayor of Baton Rouge]]{{cite news |url=https://kpel965.com/who-is-running-for-louisiana-governor-next-year-there-may-be-a-lot-of-options/ |title=Who Is Running For Louisiana Governor Next Year? The party had had a full-body meeting scheduled for October 29, but it was canceled, and instead the endorsement was voted on in an exclusive meeting held over [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]].{{cite web | url=https://www.wafb.com/2022/11/08/republicans-react-state-gop-endorsing-jeff-landry-governor/ | title=Republicans react to state GOP endorsing Jeff Landry for Governor}} Landry and [[Eddie Rispone]], a member of the Republican State Central Committee who supported him, had pushed the party to make an early endorsement, arguing that the Republicans' best chance of flipping the governorship was to unite around one candidate well in advance of the election. This move was heavily criticized by other Republicans who had expressed interest in running for governor. [[Lieutenant Governor of Louisiana|Lieutenant Governor]] [[Billy Nungesser]] said the party's endorsement process "looks more like [[Communist China (modern)|communist China]] than the Louisiana we know and love," [[Louisiana State Treasurer|State Treasurer]] [[John Schroder]] claimed it was driven by "money and inside party politics," and [[Louisiana Senate]] Majority Leader [[Sharon Hewitt]] proclaimed "the citizens of Louisiana do not need backroom deals and political insiders telling them who should be our next governor." Michael DiResto, a member of the Republican State Central Committee, believed "the idea that a small cabal would preempt the democratic process literally under the cover of darkness and in a [[smoke-filled room|smoke-filled Zoom]] goes against the foundational values of our party." In response, Louisiana Republican Party chair Louis Gurvich said "others who are crying over this endorsement are just upset because they didn't have the support within our party to win the endorsement for themselves."{{Cite web|url=https://www.theadvertiser.com/story/news/2022/11/14/john-kennedy-considers-louisiana-governors-race-poll-show-him-favored/69646074007/|title=Senator John '''Tie:''' {{legend0|#d2b1d9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} }} {{ElectionsMS}} The '''2023 Mississippi gubernatorial election''' was held on November 7, 2023, to elect the [[governor of Mississippi]]. Incumbent [[Mississippi Republican Party|Republican]] Governor [[Tate Reeves]] won re-election to a second term, defeating [[Mississippi Democratic Party|Democratic]] nominee, Public Service Commissioner [[Brandon Presley]].{{Cite web |date=2023-11-08 |title=Republican Gov. Tate Reeves wins re-election in Mississippi |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/mississippi-gov-tate-reeves-wins-re-election-extending-republicans-two-rcna122075 |access-date=2023-12-12 |website=NBC News |language=en}} This was the sixth consecutive time that a Republican was elected governor of Mississippi. Primary elections were held on August 8.{{Cite web |title=Mississippi elections, 2023 |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Mississippi_elections,_2023 |access-date=2023-01-31 |website=Ballotpedia |language=en}} Reeves won the Republican nomination, while Presley won the Democratic nomination unopposed. The race was considered to be competitive, with Reeves moderately favored. Despite Reeves winning re-election, this was the worst performance for a winning Republican, the best for a losing Democrat, and the closest Mississippi gubernatorial election since [[1999 Mississippi gubernatorial election|1999]]. It was also the closest ever gubernatorial election in the state won by a Republican,{{Cite web |last=Leip |first=Dave |title=Mississippi Election Results |url=https://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?fips=28&f=0&off=99 |access-date=November 18, 2023 |website=Dave Leip's Atlas of U.S. Presidential Elections}} and the closest gubernatorial election in the [[2023 United States gubernatorial elections|2023 cycle]]. According to [[Split Ticket (website)|Split Ticket]] estimates, Reeves won 76% of White voters while Presley won 96% of Black voters in the state.{{Cite web|url=https://split-ticket.org/2023/11/27/what-happened-in-mississippi/|title=What Happened in Mississippi|date=November 27, 2023|first1=Lakshya|last1=Jain|first2=Armin|last2=Thomas|website=Split Ticket}} {{toclimit|3}} ==Background== This was the first Mississippi gubernatorial election since a [[2020 Mississippi elections#Elimination of state electoral college|2020 referendum]] altered the election process. Previously, under a provision crafted as part of the 1890 [[Constitution of Mississippi]], a candidate needed a majority of voters across the state and a majority of voters in a majority of [[Mississippi House of Representatives|state House of Representatives]] districts; if no candidates achieved such a result, the state House of Representatives would choose between the top two finishers, something that only happened in [[1999 Mississippi gubernatorial election|1999]]. This structure was referred to as Mississippi's version of the [[United States Electoral College|electoral college]]; it was originally crafted, in the words of the Mississippi Historical Society, as part of "the legal basis and bulwark of the design of white supremacy". In the 21st century, because the state House districts favor Republican candidates, the provision was seen as helping Republican gubernatorial candidates as well.{{cite web | url=https://www.vox.com/2019/10/11/20903401/mississippi-jim-crow-law-rig-election-electoral-college-jim-hood-tate-reeves | title=How a Jim Crow law still shapes Mississippi's elections | date=October 11, 2019 }} Under the new law, any candidate who receives a majority of statewide votes will be elected; if no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, a statewide runoff election between the top two candidates will be held.{{cite web | url=https://mississippitoday.org/2020/11/04/for-the-first-time-in-state-history-voters-remove-jim-crow-provision-from-mississippi-constitution/ | title=For the first time in state history, voters remove Jim Crow provision from Mississippi Constitution | date=November 4, 2020 }} A [[Social conservatism in the United States|socially conservative]] Southern state, Mississippi is considered [[Red states and blue states|safely Republican]] at the federal and state levels, with both of its [[United States Senate|U.S. senators]], all but one of its [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] and all statewide executive officers currently belonging to the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]]. In the [[2020 United States presidential election in Mississippi|2020 presidential election]], [[Donald Trump]] comfortably carried Mississippi by 17 percentage points. Incumbent governor [[Tate Reeves]] was first elected in [[2019 Mississippi gubernatorial election|2019]], narrowly defeating then-[[Attorney General of Mississippi|attorney general]] [[Jim Hood]], who was the only [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] elected to hold statewide office in Mississippi at the time. Most analysts considered Reeves to be a favorite to win reelection, given the state's partisan lean and incumbency advantage. Nonetheless, the race was considered to be unusually competitive throughout the Fall as polling showed the race within the margin of error. Weaknesses for Reeves included his narrow victory four years prior, the heavy criticism he has faced for his handling of the [[Jackson, Mississippi, water crisis|Jackson water crisis]], and for his ties to a [[Mississippi welfare funds scandal|welfare corruption scandal]], both of which led him to have the lowest approval ratings of any Republican governor in the country. The Democratic nominee, [[Brandon Presley]], was considered to be a strong general election candidate; he represented the Northern district on the [[Mississippi Public Service Commission]] since 2008, despite that district having a strong Republican bend, and held relatively moderate views on social issues, thus being closer to fitting the state.{{Cite web |last=Vakil |first=Caroline |date=2023-01-23 |title=Democrats see Mississippi governor's race as ripe for an upset |url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/3821719-democrats-see-mississippi-governors-race-as-ripe-for-an-upset/ |access-date=2023-01-31 |website=The Hill |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |last=Lucas |first=Fred |date=2023-04-21 |title=3 deep red state governors' races that could be surprisingly competitive in 2023 — and even expand Dem control |url=https://www.foxnews.com/politics/3-very-red-state-governors-races-could-be-surprisingly-competitive-in-2023 |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=Fox News |language=en-US}} Mississippi has the highest rate of disenfranchisement in the United States and around 16% of the African American voting age population is disenfranchised.{{Cite news |date=January 8, 2022 |last=Levine |first=Sam |title=The racist 1890 law that's still blocking thousands of Black Americans from voting |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/jan/08/us-1890-law-black-americans-voting |url-status=live |archive-date=February 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240226053021/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/jan/08/us-1890-law-black-americans-voting}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Tate Reeves]], incumbent governor{{cite news |date=January 3, 2023 |title=Mississippi Republican Gov.
